common_name: Edith Wolford Bearded Iris (Award-Winning Blue-and-Yellow Bicolor Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Edith Wolford is a Dykes Medal-winning bearded iris famous for its striking blue-and-yellow bicolor pattern.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil; soggy conditions cause rhizome rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought. Introduced in 1985, Edith Wolford is one of the most celebrated bearded iris cultivars ever bred, winning the American Iris Society's top honor, the Dykes Medal, for its striking bicolor pattern of soft yellow standards over rich violet-blue falls, an unusual and eye-catching combination for the genus. Its vigorous, floriferous habit and distinctive coloring have kept it a garden and show favorite for decades. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting healthy outer fans.

common_name: Dusky Challenger Bearded Iris (Multi-Award-Winning Near-Black Purple Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Dusky Challenger is one of the most decorated bearded iris cultivars in American Iris Society history.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil; soggy conditions cause rhizome rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought. Introduced in 1986, Dusky Challenger bears huge, deep, near-black violet-purple flowers with a velvety texture and won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal along with numerous other awards, making it one of the most honored bearded iris cultivars ever released. Its exceptionally large flowers, vigorous garden performance, and dramatic dark color have kept it a benchmark dark iris for decades, both for exhibition and general garden use. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting healthy outer fans.

common_name: Rosalie Figge Bearded Iris (Ruffled White-Lavender Blend Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Rosalie Figge bears large, heavily ruffled blooms in soft white blushed with lavender.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil; soggy conditions cause rhizome rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought. Rosalie Figge bears large, heavily ruffled flowers in soft white delicately blushed with pale lavender-violet, a gentle, luminous color combination held on tall, well-branched stems above the fan of foliage. Its soft coloring and generous flower size have made it a popular garden and exhibition iris. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting healthy outer fans to maintain vigor and flowering.
